platforms.title: Thirty Pieces of Silver: The Prophecy Nobody Tried to Fulfil
platforms.description:
Five hundred years before Judas, the prophet Zechariah asked Israel to pay him his shepherd's wages. They weighed out thirty pieces of silver, the law's compensation price for a slave. And the LORD took the insult personally: "a goodly price that I was prised at of them."

Then the strangest instruction in the book: "And the LORD said unto me, Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prised at of them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them to the potter in the house of the LORD" (Zechariah 11:13, KJV).

Weighed out. Thirty pieces. Cast down. In the house of the LORD. To the potter.

Centuries later, Judas sold Jesus for exactly thirty pieces of silver, threw them down inside the temple, and the priests used the blood money to buy the potter's field (Matthew 27). Judas was not trying to fulfil a prophecy. The priests were not trying to fulfil a prophecy. Every coin still found its mark.

In this piece: the shepherd's wages in Zechariah's own story, why thirty shekels was a deliberate insult, and how the God who was priced like a slave turned the price into a purchase: his blood buying his people back.

Stop weighing out your own price. Receive his, and go free.

redteam:
VERDICT: PASS

- Verbatim check: both quoted spans ("a goodly price that I was prised at of them" and
  the full "And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them to the potter in the
  house of the LORD") are contiguous verbatim substrings of the given KJV. Clean.
- Typography: all-ASCII, no em-dashes. Clean.
- Titles: "Thirty Coins Hit the Temple Floor - 500 Years Apart" is hooky and factually
  exact (Zech ~520 BC to AD 30 is over five hundred years; the copy says "500 years
  apart" as a floor, matching the narration's own claim). No clickbait, no overclaim.
- Thread match: coins/temple/potter/field is precisely what the video delivers; the
  "nobody was trying to fulfil prophecy" line is the video's own argument, not added.
- Platform fit: TikTok/IG lead with the hook in line one, punchy; FB carries the verse;
  YT long adds the slave-price context the long description promises.
- Minor (not blocking): youtube_long tag "price of a slave bible" is awkward phrasing
  but harmless as a search key.
